notes.b: Synchronised swimming is an aesthetic water activity, one where the quality and beauty of the movement are judged as well as the skill. Swimmers link set shapes and movements into a performance to music.
points: Synchronised swimming is performing figures (set body shapes held or moved through in the water) and routines to music, either solo or in a group.
It is judged on execution (how accurately and cleanly the movements are done) and artistic impression (how well the performance is designed and presented).
The sport is now officially called artistic swimming, although the syllabus still uses the name synchronised swimming.
Swim Ireland, the national governing body for swimming, governs synchronised swimming in Ireland.
notes.tip: Synchronised swimming appears in written answers as an aesthetic activity, so be ready to use aesthetic criteria and compositional elements (the parts a performance is built from) when describing it or comparing it with other activities.

notes.b: Swimmers cannot push against the pool floor, so they hold themselves up and move using their hands. This skill is called sculling, and every position below depends on it.
points: Sculling is continuous figure-of-eight hand movement that supports and moves the body, which is why it is used throughout a routine.
Standard scull: the basic sculling movement, so it is the one to learn first.
Support scull: used in vertical positions (where the body is upside down) to hold the body up.
Propelling scull: used to move the body through the water, so the swimmer can travel across the pool.

notes.h: Back layout, front layout and tuck position
notes.b: These are the three basic body shapes. A layout is a straight, flat body held at the surface, and the tuck is its compact opposite.
points: Back layout: floating on the back, with the body straight and horizontal (flat, level with the surface).
In the back layout the face, chest, thighs and feet are at the surface.
Front layout: face down, with the body straight and horizontal at the surface.
Tuck position: the knees and hips are bent and drawn to the chest, so the body is compact (curled into a small ball).

notes.b: A pike is a position where the body folds at the hips while the legs stay straight. It can be done facing down or facing up.
points: Front pike: bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together and the trunk (the upper body) straight.
The front pike is the starting shape for many figures, so it is worth learning well.
Back pike: bent at the hips to about 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together, facing upwards, so it mirrors the front pike but on the back.

notes.b: In both of these positions the swimmer lies on her back and lifts one leg, but the other leg is placed differently.
points: Ballet leg: from the back layout, one leg is raised vertically and kept straight while the other stays at the surface.
Flamingo: a back-based position (done on the back) with one leg extended vertically, for example the same leg position as in the ballet leg.
Flamingo: the other leg is drawn up towards the chest, with the shin parallel to the surface (lying flat and level with it).

notes.b: In a vertical position the swimmer is upside down, so the legs rise out of the water. The two named variations differ in what the second leg does.
points: Vertical positions: the body is vertical and head-down, with the legs extended out of the water.
Fishtail: one leg is vertical, and the other extends forward horizontally at the surface, so only one leg is vertical.
Bent-knee vertical: one leg is vertical, and the other is bent with its toe touching the inside of the straight leg's knee.

notes.b: In an arch the back is curved. One arch is done at the surface and the other moves under the water.
points: Surface arch: the lower back is arched, with the legs at the surface, so the curve is visible above the water.
Dolphin arch: the body is arched as it travels head-first in a circle under the water, as in the dolphin figure.

notes.b: This figure turns the swimmer over by moving the legs, and it starts from two positions already covered.
points: The split walkover front begins from a front pike or a vertical position.
The legs split (open apart) and walk over to finish the figure, which is how the swimmer turns over.

notes.b: A transition is the move from one position to the next. A routine is only as good as these links, so they matter as much as the positions themselves.
points: Figures move smoothly from one position to another, without stopping or breaking the flow.
Transitions are performed with control, height (how high the body or legs rise out of the water) and stability (staying steady and balanced).

notes.b: In a duet (two swimmers) or trio (three), the positions and figures are combined into a performance. Each element below is something the performers are expected to plan.
points: Choreography: a sequence that combines the positions and figures.
Synchronisation: timing with each other and with the music, which is what gives the sport its name.
Patterns and formations, using the pool space (the swimmers arrange themselves in shapes across the pool).
Entries and exits (how the swimmers get into and out of the water).
Expression and artistic impression (showing mood and character through the performance).
notes.tip: Choreography, patterns, formations and expression are compositional elements and aesthetic criteria, so use them when asked how a performance is put together or judged.

notes.b: Performances are marked in three areas. Two are about how well the routine is done and presented, and the third is about how hard it is.
points: Execution: precision (accuracy), height, control and synchronisation.
Artistic impression: choreography, musicality (how well the movement fits the music) and manner of presentation.
Difficulty of the figures.
notes.tip: Keep execution and artistic impression separate in your answer: execution is precision, height, control and synchronisation, while artistic impression is choreography, musicality and manner of presentation.

notes.b: Synchronised swimming asks for fitness, physical skill and mental qualities all at once, because swimmers perform precise movements while upside down and holding their breath.
points: Breath control and cardio-respiratory endurance (the heart and lungs keeping working over a long routine).
Flexibility (range of movement at the joints), core strength (the trunk muscles) and leg strength.
Co-ordination (moving body parts together smoothly) and spatial awareness (knowing where you are and where others are) under water.
Concentration and teamwork, because the swimmers must stay in time with each other.

notes.b: Because swimmers spend long periods under water, safety centres on supervision and careful breath-hold training.
points: Training takes place in supervised deep water, so someone is watching in case a swimmer gets into difficulty.
Breath-hold training is built up gradually, without hyperventilation (deliberate fast over-breathing before a breath-hold).
Nose clips help keep water out of the nose, which matters when the head is under water.

keyTerms.definition: Performing figures and routines to music, either solo or in a group.
Continuous figure-of-eight hand movements that support and move the body.
A position floating flat on the front or the back, with the body straight and horizontal.
A compact position with the knees and hips bent and drawn to the chest.
A position bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with straight, together legs and a straight trunk.
A position bent at the hips to about 90 degrees, with straight, together legs, facing upwards.
A back-layout position in which one leg is raised vertically and straight while the other stays at the surface.
A vertical position with one leg vertical and the other extended forward horizontally at the surface.
A back-based position with one leg vertical and the other drawn up, its shin parallel to the surface.
A position with the lower back arched and the legs at the surface.
A position in which the body is arched as it travels head-first in a circle under the water.
A figure in which the legs split and walk over from a front pike or vertical position to finish.

factCards.term: Name the three types of scull
factCards.definition: Standard scull, support scull (in vertical positions) and propelling scull.

factCards.term: What angle is the hip bent to in a front pike?
factCards.definition: 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together and the trunk straight.

factCards.term: What does execution cover in judging?
What does artistic impression cover in judging?
factCards.definition: Choreography, musicality and manner of presentation.

questions.prompt: Describe three positions used in synchronised swimming and explain what judges look for in each.
questions.model: Front pike: the body is bent at the hips to 90 degrees, with the legs straight and together and the trunk straight. It is the starting shape for many figures. Judges look for precision in the angle and in the straightness of the legs and trunk, and for height and control as the position is entered and held. Back layout: the body floats on the back, straight and horizontal, with the face, chest, thighs and feet at the surface. Judges look for a straight, horizontal line held with control and stability. Ballet leg: from the back layout, one leg is raised vertically and kept straight while the other stays at the surface. Judges look for a straight, vertical leg held with height and control and, in a duet or trio, synchronisation with the partners.

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of sculling in synchronised swimming.
questions.model: Sculling is a continuous figure-of-eight hand movement that supports and moves the body. The support scull holds the body up in vertical positions, so the performer can keep the upper body out of the water without sinking. The propelling scull moves the body through the water, which lets the performer travel between positions and across the pool. Without sculling, the performer could not hold the vertical shapes or move smoothly through a routine.
